Rubric rule 13: "a jurisdiction whose dossier shows (i) no trans-specific criminal offence, (ii) no documented targeting of trans people by police, border officers or violence, and (iii) documented social acceptance of gender diversity (an embedded third-gender tradition or equivalent) sits above jurisdictions with similar formal machinery but no documented acceptance — and only moderately below jurisdictions documenting both comparable acceptance AND working protections."

The 0.65-C/0.75-C/0.85-C anchors are exactly this shape. 0.85-C and 0.75-C have documented positive service evidence, courts awarding compensation, facilities accommodating by identity. Here we have none of that — no documented protections working, no documented service evidence, no current social data. That's the difference between the 0.65-C anchor (which has ordinary courts awarding compensation, no visitor-service complaint system) and this dossier.

The caveats: the trans-relevant data is essentially absent. Under rule 13's weighting: known exposures — none documented (an unenforced tangential statute is light); open questions — many (border, custody, facilities, care); resident gaps — no LGR, no anti-discrimination. Open questions are "far lighter" weight than known exposures. So the absence of trans-specific documentation shouldn't drag it down heavily.

But rule 3 & 13 say documented positives count and thin-data doesn't resolve to midpoint. Here we have a documented positive: embedded third-gender tradition (documented in sources). Plus no trans-specific criminal offence, no documented targeting. That's the rule-13 pattern that sits above jurisdictions with similar machinery but no documented acceptance.

Also the unenforced sodomy statute: rule 2 — in a jurisdiction with documented tolerant social framing of gender diversity, a dead-letter statute is a tangential signal, must not dominate.

However, there is essentially no evidence about the visitor-facing infrastructure: border, hotels, facilities, custody, emergency care. In a small island state, a trans visitor's presentation may be read as local cultural role rather than threat — mildly positive.

I'd put this slightly below the 0.65-C anchor given the thinner record and the decade-old data, no documented working remedy or current acceptance measurement. Perhaps 0.60? Or around 0.62-0.65.

This dossier: traditional acceptance documented (weaker, "cultural roles not legal status"), dead-letter statute, no protections at all documented, no current climate data, government considering anti-discrimination law (positive), pro-SOGI UN vote (positive).

Missing: any court/regulatory action, any foreign-passport acceptance data, any service evidence.

Also no evidence of hostility either — 2015 report recorded no societal discrimination; the only hostile claim (lesbians face violence) is unsourced and not carried.

So the worst documented feature is roughly (5) paper protections not shown to operate, plus an unenforced statute. That's relatively mild. But the absence of any trans-specific evidence at all means many open questions, and openness in a small jurisdiction with a criminalising statute plus no LGR and no anti-discrimination machinery resolves toward modest risk per rule 13's "thin-data" guidance — though also the traditional role is a documented positive.

I think 0.62 is defensible, but the calibration anchor 0.65-C matches fairly well and has more documentation. Let me settle on 0.60.
